subject: rocket launch
title: What If You Stood Next to a Rocket Launch? The Sound Hits First

scenes.text: What if you stood beside a launching rocket? The sound would break you before the fire did.
Start far away. When NASA's Moon rocket lifted off in 2022, microphones 1.5 kilometres out read 136 decibels. Louder than a jet engine.
At 5 kilometres, where reporters stand, 129 decibels, the edge of physical pain. The air crackled like fireworks.
Now walk to the pad. A Saturn V hit about 203 decibels. Every 10 decibels is ten times the energy: millions of times the viewing stands.
Your eardrums give out around 150. By 200, the pressure swings slam your chest and lungs like a wall of air.
The myth says a Saturn V melted concrete a mile away. It didn't. It wouldn't melt the ground under you. You'd be the first thing it broke.

description:
What if you stood beside a rocket as it launched? Measurements of NASA's Artemis I launch put the noise at about 136 decibels 1.5 kilometres away and about 129 decibels at the 5-kilometre press site, around the threshold of pain, with a crackling quality from shock waves in the exhaust.
At the pad itself the Saturn V produced roughly 203 decibels. Since every 10 decibels means ten times the acoustic energy, that is millions of times the energy reaching the viewing stands; eardrums rupture around 150 decibels and pressure swings near 200 decibels can injure the lungs. Acoustics researchers have shown the old claims that the Saturn V melted concrete or set grass on fire a mile away are myths.

first_comment: The water deluge system on a launch pad isn't mainly for cooling: hundreds of thousands of litres are dumped to soak up sound and protect the rocket from its own noise. Where would you want to watch a launch from?
